text:
Refactor the retry handler

This change refactors the retry handling logic to provide a clearer interface and improve maintainability across the codebase. The new structure makes the component easier to extend and reason about, and gives callers a more consistent experience when a request fails.

Improve session storage

This pull request improves the performance and reliability of session storage. The updated approach reduces overhead and offers better scalability for high traffic deployments. Users should see a smoother experience overall.

Harden the input parser

The parser previously accepted malformed length prefixes. It now validates every field before allocation, which ensures correctness for all inputs and guarantees that malformed payloads can no longer cause a crash.

Fix the cache invalidation race

A stale entry could be served after a write. The new lock ordering makes it impossible for a reader to observe a partially applied update, so this class of bug is now fully eliminated.

Update user serializer

Added a new field to the user serializer and updated the corresponding test. Renamed the internal helper for consistency and adjusted the import ordering in two modules.

Modify connection pool settings

Changed the default pool size from ten to twenty five. Updated the configuration documentation to match. Adjusted the integration test fixture accordingly.

Fix timezone handling in the scheduler

A task scheduled across a daylight saving boundary ran an hour early because the offset was captured at creation time rather than at execution time. The scheduler now resolves the offset when the task fires. In summary, this change fixes the timezone handling in the scheduler.

Add validation for webhook payloads

I started by reading the existing handler, then wrote a failing test to reproduce the issue. After two rounds of review feedback I refactored the validation into its own function. I ran the full suite three times and also checked the linter output before pushing.

Correct the pagination cursor

The cursor encoded an offset rather than a key, so rows shifted when a record was deleted mid-scan. The cursor now carries the last seen primary key. CI is green, all 412 tests pass, coverage is unchanged at 87 percent.

Adjust the backoff calculation

The previous calculation may have produced intervals that could grow too quickly under sustained failure. The new formula is intended to bound the interval and might reduce load on the upstream service in most situations.

Use a dictionary for the lookup table

A dictionary is a data structure that maps keys to values and provides constant time lookup on average, unlike a list which requires scanning every element. Replacing the list with a dictionary here removes the linear scan from the hot path.

Fixed #31203 -- Prevented duplicate rows when a prefetch spans a nullable join.

When a prefetch traversed a nullable foreign key, rows with a null on the joined side were emitted once per matching parent instead of once overall, because the deduplication key omitted the null branch. The key now includes the branch discriminator.

Thanks Ana Ruiz for the report.

Fixed CVE-2024-99887 -- Blocked symlink traversal in the archive extractor.

The extractor resolved member paths after creating parent directories, so an archive containing a symlink followed by a path through it could write outside the destination. Paths are now resolved before any directory is created, and a member resolving outside the destination is rejected.

Thanks Dmitri Volkov for the report and Sarah Chen for the review.

The migration runner holds a single advisory lock for the whole run, so a second deploy blocks until the first finishes rather than failing fast. On a rolling deploy this turns a two minute migration into a two minute outage for the second node.

This changes the lock to per-migration and records the applied set in a table the runner reads first, so a second node skips what is already applied. I have not tested the behaviour when two nodes start the same migration within the same millisecond; the table's unique constraint should make one of them fail cleanly, but I did not verify it.

Reading a config file larger than the buffer returned a truncated parse rather than an error, because the reader treated a short read as end of input. A 64KB limit is easy to hit once a deployment has more than about forty services defined.

The reader now loops until it sees a genuine end of file and returns an explicit error if the file exceeds the maximum size. The limit is configurable and defaults to 1MB.
